title: Why You Must Require Properly Spoken Language In Your Classroom
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin makes the case that requiring clear, properly spoken language in the classroom is not outdated or discriminatory but a genuine service to students, since strong spoken communication carries real advantages in employment, respect, influence, confidence, and even written skill. He acknowledges the common objections -- that the standard is subjective or culturally biased -- but argues the goal isn't to prescribe how the world should be, only to equip students with a practical advantage given how the world actually judges speech. He connects spoken and written skill directly, arguing that grammatically sound speech is the foundation written composition builds on, and frames the growing reluctance among teachers to correct student speech as a disservice rather than a kindness.
points: Strong spoken communication is framed as a direct employment and influence advantage, regardless of profession, and worth teaching explicitly.
People judge speaking ability quickly and often unfairly; equipping students with clear, confident speech is presented as arming them against that reality.
Spoken language forms the foundation of written language: students who can't speak in proper grammatical structure will struggle to write that way.
The goal is framed as adding 'another arrow in the quiver' for students, not asserting how the world should be, in response to objections that the standard is discriminatory.
quotes: But with the right touch and spirit of compassion, you’re only helping your students by encouraging clear and universally understood spoken language.
Once in the real world, the ability to communicate well—no matter the profession—is an employment advantage. Clarity and brevity equal more success and better pay.
People judge. They judge harshly, unfairly, and based on superficials. Just the way it is.
The way we speak forms the foundation of how we write. If you’re unable to speak using proper grammatical structure, then doing so in written form is impossible.
I’m arguing that this is how the world is and we shouldn’t pretend that the way that many of our students speak in professional settings, like the classroom, isn’t going to affect them.
